summary: A 1975 note on the difference between early and later versions of FTP, arguing for leaving well enough alone. It is part of a discussion thread that includes RFC 691, RFC 640, RFC 630, RFC 542, RFC 454, RFC 448, RFC 414, RFC 385 and RFC 354.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 686 argues that the network should improve the FTP version most hosts already use instead of waiting for a new version to take over. It proposes several changes to reply codes and file-handling rules.

questions: early ftp versus later ftp differences
what did rfc 686 propose for ftp
what changes did rfc 686 propose for ftp
subtitle: An argument for fixing FTP-1 rather than waiting for widespread FTP-2 adoption.

tldr.problem: Brian Harvey says nearly all hosts still use FTP-1, while FTP-2's existence is being used as a reason to postpone fixes to the version in use.
tldr.mechanism: He evaluates the claimed advantages of FTP-2 and proposes changes to FTP-1 reply handling, HELP and STAT responses, experimental codes, and print-file behavior.
tldr.outcome: RFC 686 is an opinion and proposal for discussion; it suggests making several improvements without requiring a wholesale move to FTP-2.

today: The unit records RFC 686's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It is a proposal to improve FTP-1 without requiring an immediate transition to FTP-2.

sections.title: Why Keep Improving FTP-1
sections.content:
Brian Harvey describes starting an overhaul of his site's FTP programs and finding that hosts implemented the protocol differently. He says that, as far as he could tell, all but one network host ran FTP-1 and transferred files successfully.

His position is that an unused protocol document should not block maintenance of the protocol in use unless the new version is imminent or clearly superior. He reviews FTP-2's differences and asks whether their benefits justify reprogramming.
sections.plainLanguage: The author says most hosts are using FTP-1 and transferring files. He would rather fix problems in that version than wait for a new one that is not in use.

sections.title: Evaluating FTP-2's Changes
sections.content:
Harvey argues that some FTP-2 features have limited value for file-transfer programs, that the print-file rules can be clarified within FTP-1, and that a network virtual file system raises compatibility questions. He prefers putting detailed error explanations in reply text and says reply-code revisions can be adapted without requiring every host to reprogram at once.

He also questions switching merely because a committee approved FTP-2, because its document is online while FTP-1's is not, or to change MODE and STRU behavior. He says individual problems, such as TENEX paged-file transfers, can be addressed within the current framework.
sections.plainLanguage: The author reviews eight reasons for adopting FTP-2 and says most do not justify a major change for every host. He supports clearer rules and targeted fixes for problems users actually encounter.

sections.title: Reply Codes and Proposed Changes
sections.content:
The author describes a simple way an FTP user program might interpret reply codes: the first digit generally indicates information, success or failure, with a few special cases for codes beginning with 3. He identifies inconsistent responses to HELP as a problem and proposes that HELP end with reply 200.

Other proposals define 1xx replies as informational, limit experimental codes to the x9x or xx9 forms below 600, clarify STAT behavior, and specify that the recipient reformats TYPE P and F files if needed. He also proposes moving many 4xx replies to 5xx to distinguish permanent from temporary failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The first digit of an FTP reply can help a program decide whether a command succeeded. The author wants servers to use that rule consistently, including for HELP, STAT and experimental replies.

sections.title: The Reply-Code Table
sections.content:
The RFC ends with a table mapping current FTP-1 replies to the author's proposed numbers. Examples include changing the rename-success reply from 253 to 223, the delete-success reply from 254 to 224, and the file-not-found reply from 450 to 520.

Harvey says changes from 4xx to 5xx should be required as of June 1, while changes to the second or third digit are less important. He notes that there is no formal mechanism in the protocol for adopting his plan.
sections.plainLanguage: A table at the end shows the reply numbers Harvey wants to change. He proposes a date for required temporary-versus-permanent changes but acknowledges the plan is not formally adopted.
